extracted.intended_audience: math olympiad organizers, coaches, and contestants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critique on designing scoring rubrics for math-olympiad problems so they reward genuine problem solving, resist gaming/exploitation, and balance partial credit versus full-solution incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward complete solutions; keep partials small (0+/7- property)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer rubrics where a full solution clearly yields the full score (e.g. 7 points) and partial credit for incomplete work is small — the '0+/7-' style where the winning strategy is to maximize fully solved problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that clean 0+/7- rubrics make the winning strategy obvious (maximize solved problems) and reduce meta-analysis. Small partials should correspond to genuinely helpful work already done in pursuit of a solution rather than creating incentives to hunt for rubric crumbs. This reduces coaching toward gaming the marking scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid totally additive/chunked rubrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide the problem's total points into many independent additive chunks that sum to the final score (i.e. fully additive marking schemes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additive rubrics are usually more generous and create more 'surface area' for exploitation; examples include splitting two-part problems into halves so one can score many small guaranteed points. The author notes increasing prevalence of additive schemes (e.g. at IMO) and that they tend to invite meta-gaming and score inflation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'exploitable' rubric
rubrics_metrics.description: A rubric is 'exploitable' if knowing what the rubric is encourages you to do something else (i.e., change behavior to maximize points rather than to solve problems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post emphasizes that even if full understanding of a rubric requires knowing solutions, seeing many past rubrics by the same author effectively provides exploitable knowledge. Repeated exposure (precedents across years) exacerbates this. Designing against exploitation means ensuring rubric knowledge doesn't create a profitable meta-strategy distinct from solving the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourage rewarding isolated special cases or 'easy crumbs'
rubrics_metrics.description: Rubrics should not incentivize contestants to spend time extracting trivial or isolated observations (e.g., checking n=1,2,... special cases) with no intention of solving the general problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author gives examples of first-time contestants looking for rubric items to extract points and experienced contestants breadth-first searching for easy crumbs. Rubrics that reward many small observations encourage a meta-game of 'how much time to spend writing down every easy observation I can think of' rather than pursuing complete solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not give partial credit for incomplete analytic/coordinate-bashing approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Incomplete analytic setups (e.g., starting coordinate bashing and not finishing) should not routinely receive partial credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post provides the Alice vs Bob thought experiment: reward the contestant who recognizes a path is impractical and abandons it (Alice), not the one who dives into long hopeless calculations (Bob). If partials were routinely given, coaches would train students to always write down setups and plunge into calculations even when unlikely to finish, increasing low-value work and gaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish rubrics only when they are not exploitable
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about releasing full rubrics publicly: publish them for contests where the rubrics are not exploitable, avoid publishing when doing so would teach coaches/contestants to game itemized partials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author is comfortable publishing USEMO rubrics (because they are non-exploitable) but wary of publishing IMO rubrics since explicit items (e.g., 'proving that a_i=0 is not possible: 1 point') would prompt coaches to direct students to pursue those items. Transparency is good in principle, but publishing exploitable rubrics trains unwanted behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer structural fixes (more/ easier problems) over generous partial credit to reduce discouragement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the aim is to reduce discouragement among less-experienced students, consider changing test structure (e.g., more problems, including easier ones) rather than inflating partial credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author suggests a 4-problem test with two easy problems as an alternative to giving generous partial credit: it provides more chances to solve whole problems without changing the incentive structure that rewards complete solutions. This avoids score inflation while helping less-experienced students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design rubrics with repeated-game/precedent effects in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that rubrics form precedents: rubrics in a given year influence behavior in future years, so design choices have long-term, cumulative effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because contestants and coaches learn from past rubrics (having seen many past rubrics by the same person is akin to 'knowing' the rubric), designers should avoid creating item patterns that will be learned and exploited over time. This long-run perspective argues for resisting small-itemization and against publishing exploitable details.
